The American pygmy kingfisher (Chloroceryle aenea) is one of the smallest members of the Alcedinidae, a fact reflected in its modest adult body dimensions. Field measurements indicate that females attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 15 grams [Wwi = approximately 15 grams], a figure consistent with the upper range reported for this species in the literature. Males are slightly lighter on average, with an ultimate wet weight reaching about 14.9 grams [Wwi = about 14.9 grams], illustrating a subtle but detectable sexual size dimorphism that is typical of many kingfisher species where females are the larger sex. This minor difference in mass likely corresponds to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The basal metabolic rate of this species has been quantified in respirometry trials, revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 31.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a value that aligns with predictions for a non-passerine bird of this diminutive size.

This annual reproductive effort is modest when compared to larger, multi-brooded kingfisher species, but it is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival through extended parental care. The time from hatching to fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest cavity, is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of small-bodied kingfishers that face high predation pressure on their nest sites.

This lifespan is intermediate for a bird of its body size; smaller passerines often have shorter maximum ages, while some larger kingfishers can exceed a decade. The relatively modest longevity is likely influenced by the high predation rates faced by this species from arboreal snakes, raptors, and mammalian predators that frequent riparian habitats.
